title: Chapter 95 – The Inner Court
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The Inner Court measures a man before it feeds him.

On the ninth morning Jian stands in a long cold room called the Hall of Weights, in his gray tunic and the white jade tag, barefoot on a floor of black tile, and waits for a clerk to finish writing his name. The clerk is young and fast and does not look up. The brush scratches. A brazier in the corner gives out more smoke than heat. In the center of the room, on a plinth of the same black stone as the Dock, a disc of bronze the width of a table turns slowly on a pin.

It is called the Mirror of Weights. It is not the Outer Court's Mirror, the one that read him Qi Refining ninth rank in front of two hundred witnesses. That Mirror measured a single thing. This one measures three.

"Step on the plate," says the man beside the plinth.

He is tall, thin, and graying at the temples, with the shoulders of a man who has spent years bending over papers. His robe is a darker gray than the others', with a narrow silver edge. Jian knows his face. Cheng Yun, the Inspector who audited the Green Pine Garden in the summer. Honest, scrupulous, and the man who, in the end, walked Zhao Qian into custody with her ruined wrist.

"Inspector Cheng."

"Not Inspector." The thin man's smile is small and without humor. "Deputy Examiner of the Hall of Weights, this season. The floor restored me one rank beneath where I stood. It is a fair penalty. I let a Blood Shadow work under my nose for a year." He nods at the plate. "Step on."

Jian steps on. The bronze is cold under his bare feet. The disc turns, and begins to hum.

* * *

He has prepared for this. It is the only thing he has been able to prepare for.

Nine days in the Inner Court, nine nights with a slip of white paper under his mattress, and on every one of them he has lain awake and rehearsed. The Mirror cannot be fooled. The Veil that once hid his root and his Qi died in the fog of the Wellmaster's trap, and he has not rebuilt it. He has CE zero. The Spring Vein is a dead cord in his arm. What the Mirror will read is what he is.

A Foundation Early cultivator, age twenty-one. On the strength of the base alone, it is an astonishing thing. Most disciples reach Foundation at thirty, and most never. It will be written down in a ledger, and the ledger will be read.

Better that than a lie the Mirror can catch.

The disc turns. Three rings of light rise from its surface, one above the other, and settle in the air in front of his chest. The first is white. The second is a dull red. The third is a pale, clear blue.

"Qi," says Cheng Yun, reading. "Foundation Establishment, early stage. Step five." His pen pauses. "Body. Qi Refining peak. Step four. Soul." A beat. "Qi Refining peak. Step four."

The clerk's brush has stopped.

"That is a surprise," says Cheng Yun quietly. He does not look up from his page. "In my twenty-two years in this Hall, I have seen four disciples cross into Foundation before thirty. You will be the fifth to be written down, and the youngest by eight years. The spread is one step. That is a good frame. A very good frame." He glances at the plinth. "You did not tell the floor."

"The floor did not ask."

"No." The man writes it down. "I am obliged to ask now. Did you break through in the Dock?"

"Before it. Nine days before."

"Then it is not a Founders' gift."

"No, Inspector. Examiner." Jian keeps his eyes on the rings. "It was a cold-water chamber and a good deal of root soup. My brother can confirm it."

Cheng Yun's mouth twitches. He puts the pen down.

"I will record it as a natural breakthrough, aided by the Stillness Chamber and the Pill Hall," he says. "That is true. It is also enough." He holds Jian's eye a moment longer than he needs to. "I would advise you to be less true than you are, from here on. The Hall of Weights reports to the Sutra Hall, and the Sutra Hall reports to the floor. Not everything in this building is as honest as I am."

He closes the ledger. The rings fade.

"Your cell has a stove. Go and warm yourself. You look as though you have not stopped shaking since the stair."

"Yes, Examiner."

He steps off the plate and finds that Cheng Yun is right. His knees are not steady, and the hand he lays on the plinth to hold himself up leaves a damp print on the black stone that fades even as he looks at it. A Foundation base only weeks old, he thinks, and the world has already started to measure it.

* * *

The Inner Court has tiers, and it does not hide them.

They are explained to him by a steward over a breakfast of millet and pickled radish in the long hall by the frozen pool. There are five. At the bottom, Bronze Leaf: disciples newly promoted, in their first year, under a probationary tutor. Above them, Silver Leaf, the established disciples with a Foundation base, who may take missions outside the Sect with a pass. Then Jade Leaf, those in the middle stages, who may sit in the lower vaults. Gold Leaf, who may sit in the upper. And at the very top, in a house on the ridge that the steward lowers his voice to name, the Sect's Sealed disciples, who answer to no Elder but the one in seclusion.

"You are Silver Leaf," says the steward. He is a small man, stooped, with kind tired eyes. "By the Hall's ruling, since you are Foundation. Provisional, of course. You are also Gate-tagged, which is not a tier, and which no one has quite worked out how to handle. The Rule has no article for it." He sips his tea. "My advice is to do exactly as Elder Ye says and ask her nothing."

"That is Bai's advice too."

"Bai is wise when it comes to Ye."

There are tutors. Jian is given three of them, assigned by a list pinned to the hall door. For the body, a heavy, silent woman named Kuang who teaches the Iron Bone drill at dawn on the frozen lawn. For Qi, a thin man with a stammer called Ouyang, who sets the Silver Leaf disciples to breathe in the cold until their lips go blue. For the soul, in the afternoon, a lecture in the Hall of Quiet by Elder Ye herself, in front of fifteen young faces turned up like cups.

He sits near the back. He listens to her explain the nine steps of soul refinement in a clear dry voice, from the first thread of awareness to the sea that will one day hold the whole world. He writes nothing, because he has a memory that does not need it. And he keeps his face still, because he sits two seats from a girl with a flat black braid who has been watching him since the lecture began.

* * *

Iron Bone begins before the sun.

Kuang does not speak on the frozen lawn. She stands in the blue dark with her arms folded, a woman built like a gatepost, and lets the Silver Leaf disciples find their own places on the ice. They number eleven. Jian takes the last spot, between a lanky boy with frostbitten ears and a stocky girl who yawns without covering her mouth. Then Kuang lifts a hand, and the drill begins.

It is not complicated. A man stands in a low stance, arms out, and a second man strikes him with a wooden pole across the thighs, the ribs, the back. The drill is to take the blows and breathe. Each strike sets the bone ringing. Each ring, if the breath is right, drives a little of the body's dross out through the skin. The pole is hard. The ground is harder. By the sixth strike his breath is a rag.

Body, step four, he thinks, through the white haze of it. One behind the Qi. It will not be allowed to fall further.

The soul vessel aches behind his eyes. The crack he saw on the bench is a faint heat now, running from crown to heart. He does not use the Seal. He cannot. He bears the strikes the way he bore the cold water in the Stillness Chamber, one at a time, counting.

When it ends, the frost on his tunic has melted and frozen again. Kuang walks down the line, looking at each man's stance. At Jian she stops.

"Your bones are wrong," she says. It is the first thing she has said.

He waits.

"They are too clean." Her flat eyes search his face. "A man at your stage should have a little black in the marrow. The dross of the old body. You do not. Someone has been washing you." She grunts. "I do not ask who. Tomorrow I will hit harder."

"Yes, Tutor."

"And eat more. You are a bag of sticks."

She turns away. The boy with the frostbitten ears lets out a long unsteady breath, and says to nobody, with deep feeling: "She said nothing to me for three months."

* * *

"You are thinner than I expected," says Tan Ruyan.

She finds him after the lecture, in the colonnade, where the wind off the ridge comes down between the pillars like a blade. She is nineteen now, taller than he remembers, with the same straight-backed way of standing that made her a prodigy in the Trial. She wears the silver-edged gray of a Silver Leaf and a single jade pin, and the pin is new. She passed the Inner Court entrance in the fall, he knows, at the top of her cohort. She has not yet said a single word to him that was not a courtesy.

"I have been told."

"By everyone." She does not smile. "I did not come to say that. I came to say that I am glad you are alive, and that I am not surprised."

"Not surprised?"

"You were thirty-eight on the stair, and you stopped because you chose to stop. I was on forty-one. I do not think you chose to stop." Her eyes are level and dark. "I have been thinking about that since the Trial. About what it means to stop at a place you could have passed."

He says nothing. The wind pulls at his cloak.

"I will not ask," says Tan Ruyan. "You owe me no answer. I owe you a favor, and I have not forgotten it. I will tell you what I know, and you may do with it what you like." She steps closer, lowers her voice. "The Inner Court has more eyes than you think. Not the Sutra Hall's. Not Enforcement's. Another set. They are polite, and they are everywhere, and none of them ever asks you a question." Her gaze flicks to the colonnade's far end, to the long low door of a clerk's office. "My family sells reagents to the Sect, Lin Jian. We have a great deal to do with the accounts. In four years I have never once been able to tell you who reads them."

"Why are you telling me?"

"Because you went into the Founders' chamber, and you came out. And whoever the eyes belong to, they will want to know why."

She nods to him, once, correct and cool, and walks away along the colonnade with her braid swinging. He watches her go.

A debt remembered, he thinks. And a warning that costs her more than she lets on.

* * *

He tells Ye about the note.

It is the thirteenth night, and he has put it off as long as a man can. He climbs the winding stair to the Sutra Hall's upper floor after the evening bell, with the white square folded in his sleeve, and finds her at her desk in a room lined floor to ceiling with scrolls. A single lamp burns. She does not look up when he comes in.

"It is late."

"You said I should tell you if anything unusual happened."

"I did."

He lays the paper on her desk. She looks at it for a long moment without touching it. Then she takes a lens from her sleeve, a disc of crystal as thin as a leaf, and bends over it.

"Where?"

"On my pillow. On the night I came into the Inner Court. I was asleep."

"Was the door locked?"

"I do not know. I did not lock it."

"Hm." The lens moves across the page, slowly, left to right. "The paper is plum-bark. It is made in the Inner Court's own mill and used only by its clerks. You cannot buy it outside the wall." Her voice has gone very quiet. "The ink is common. The hand is trained. A clerk's hand, drilled for thirty years. You see the loops on the d, and the way the stroke lifts at the end of each word. There are perhaps forty people in the Inner Court who write like that."

"Forty."

"It is a smaller number than I would like." She straightens. She does not look frightened. She looks, in the lamplight, like a woman who has found the first loose thread in a robe she has been mending for forty years. "Welcome back, Operator. You know what that means."

He weighs the question. A wrong answer could close a door he needs.

"I know what it means to me," he says slowly. "I do not know what it means to them."

Ye takes a long time to answer.

"It means," she says at last, "that someone in this building has been watching the Gate for far longer than you have been alive. That they were not surprised when it opened. And that they have a name for the person it opens for, which is not Bearer." She sets down the lens. "That is what I think. I would be glad to be wrong."

"What do I do?"

"You do nothing. You sleep with your door barred and your animal on the pillow. You say nothing to Enforcement, because Enforcement has its own clerks. You say nothing to anyone." She folds the paper once, neatly, and slides it into a drawer. "And you come to me again, the moment it happens a second time."

"It will happen a second time?"

"A man who leaves one note," says Elder Ye, "has more to say."

* * *

The pill costs four hundred and twenty stones, and he has forty-one to his name.

He does the arithmetic on the fourteenth morning, at his low table, with the brazier ticking and the ice outside the window going gold in the sun. He has no points, because the points are frozen. He has no pay, because Silver Leaf stipend is a month away. He has what he came with: a knife, a flint, a flask, a little black book. Two Moon-ash lotus buds from Han, one of them already half-promised to a Garden stall. One gray Nine Turn pill, which is for him and no one else.

And a brother who sits in a cave on Terrace Four with the Qi at the door and no way through.

He sets the pill aside. It is not for sale. He lifts the lotus bud out of its paper wrap and looks at it for a while. It is a lovely thing, the size of a thumbnail, pale violet-white, with a faint cold light at its heart. Han gave it to him for a day's work, and it would take a decade to grow another.

Every advantage has a cost, he thinks. This one costs me a bud.

He finds Tan Ruyan at her family's stall on the Inner Court's market row, a narrow wooden counter with a canopy of blue cloth and a rack of sealed jars. She is not there. Her uncle is, a heavyset man with a trader's soft hands and a ledger the size of a door. He looks at the bud for a long, long time through a glass.

"Four hundred and fifty," says the uncle.

"It is worth nine hundred."

"In the south, in the right season, to the right buyer. Here, in winter, with a Gate tag on the seller's neck and the whole market watching?" He lays the glass down. "Four hundred and fifty. I will throw in the Foundation pill at cost, and a tonic for the buyer's meridians. That is the best I can do, and I am doing it because my niece told me to."

Jian considers. The uncle is right about the tag. Everyone in the row has found a reason to glance at the white jade at his throat.

"Four hundred and fifty," he says. "And the pill to my brother's name, not mine. No ledger entry."

The man's eyebrow lifts. Then he nods, and writes something small on a slip, and does not put it in the ledger.

When the transaction is done, Jian walks the length of the row with the pill in his sleeve, a tiny lacquer box warm from the uncle's hand. It is the first time in his life that he has spent something precious on someone else without a ledger. It weighs almost nothing. He is aware of the eyes on his back at every step, and of a quieter fact beneath it: the Tan family now holds a bud of Moon-ash lotus that came from his hand, and a ledger entry that says nothing. In a market, a silence like that is also a kind of price. He will be asked for it, one day, in the coin of an introduction or a name.

* * *

Terrace Four has a cave on its north face where a man can sit out of the wind.

Feng is there at noon, as Qinghe said he would be. The mouth of the cave is hung with a curtain of felt, and the inside smells of stone and old sweat. A pallet, a water jar, a half-eaten bowl of cold rice. In the center of the floor, cross-legged, with his hands on his knees and his eyes shut, his brother sits in the posture of the First Door, and his breath is slow and even and a little too careful.

"You are early," says Feng, without opening his eyes.

"I have something for you."

"I do not want charity."

"It is not charity." Jian sits down opposite him, crossing his legs with an effort that makes his ribs complain. "It is a loan. You will pay me back."

Feng opens his eyes. They are dark and steady and very tired. He looks at the lacquer box in Jian's palm, and for a long moment does not move at all.

"What is it?"

"A Rising Tide pill. The standard. Four hundred and twenty stones, at cost."

"I know what it costs." His brother's voice is low. "I have been doing that sum for a month. You have no stones. You have no points. You have been in the Inner Court nine days. Where did you get it?"

"I sold something."

"What?"

"A flower."

"What flower?"

"A good one."

The silence goes on. Feng's jaw works. He reaches out, picks up the box, and turns it over in his big scarred fingers, and Jian sees that his hand is shaking, very slightly.

"I have thought of this pill," Feng says, "every night for a month. I have lain awake and thought of how it would taste." He swallows. "I had decided that I would wait until I earned it. That I would take a mission, a long one, outside. That I would not ask my brother for what a man ought to earn himself."

"You are the first-ranked of the Outer Court. You have earned it four times over."

"The Outer Court gives a medal for that, Jian. It does not give a pill."

"Then take mine." He keeps his voice level. "I did not earn the bud. Han gave it to me for a day's labor and I did not deserve it. I turned it into a thing that you can use. That is all I did. Do not make a debt of it."

Feng looks at him for a very long time.

Then he opens the box, takes out the pill, a dull amber bead the size of a pea, and puts it in his mouth before he can think better of it. He swallows. He closes his eyes.

"It is bitter."

"Yes."

"Is it supposed to burn?"

"Yes. Breathe."

Heat comes up in the cave like the opening of a furnace door. Jian feels it on his face, and then something deeper, a slow gathering pressure that makes the air thick. Feng's chest rises and falls. His fists have closed. A drop of sweat runs from his temple to his jaw, and then another, and then the stone beneath him begins, very faintly, to hum.

The Qi is at the door, Jian thinks. It is coming through.

He sits with his brother for three hours, and does not speak. When the light in the cave has gone from white to gold, Feng makes a low sound in his throat, and the humming stops.

He opens his eyes. They are different. Not brighter. Deeper.

"Foundation," says Lin Feng, in a voice that is hardly a voice. "Early stage." He stares at his own hands. "I am twenty-seven, and I am Foundation. Father will not believe it."

"He will."

"Jian." Feng's face works, and he gives up trying to hold it. "I owe you."

"You owe me the price of the pill," says Jian. "Mother will keep the ledger."

His brother laughs, a cracked, astonished, helpless sound. It is the first time Jian has heard it in a year.

* * *

On the way back up from the terraces, at the far end of the colonnade, between the clerks' offices and the stair to the bell tower, there is a door he has passed fourteen times and never looked at.

It is a plain door, of dark wood, in a plain wall. There is a lamp beside it, and under the lamp, a small black board with a single line of white characters painted in a neat hand.

Office of the Registry.

He had taken it for the Sect's ordinary roll office. The place where tokens are issued, where names are entered, where tags are struck. A dull place. A place to walk past.

The door is ajar. He slows, because he cannot help it. In the narrow gap he can see a long bright room with high windows, a dozen desks, a dozen clerks bent over their work. Rows of shelves behind them, rising to the ceiling, stacked with ledgers bound in gray. A smell of ink and plum bark.

At the nearest desk, a young man is copying a list. Jian can see the page from where he stands. The hand is small and exact. The loops on the d are closed. The stroke lifts at the end of each word.

He does not stop walking. He does not turn his head. He passes the door as he has passed it fourteen times, and goes on along the colonnade toward the bell tower and his cell, with an empty sleeve and a hard cold place in his chest where the Seal is beating.

Beware the ones who wear no names.

Behind him, in the bright room, the young clerk does not look up. But his brush, for one moment, hesitates over the page.
